chapter_text:
CHAPTER 4 - CELL: STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION

Introduction

Every living thing you can name - a towering banyan tree, a buzzing mosquito, the bacterium in a drop of pond water, and you yourself - is built from cells. The cell is the smallest unit that can carry out all the activities we associate with life: it takes in nutrients, releases energy, grows, responds to its surroundings, and reproduces. Some organisms are a single cell (unicellular), while others such as human beings are made of trillions of cells (multicellular). This chapter examines what a cell is, how the cell theory came to be, the two great classes of cells (prokaryotic and eukaryotic), the differences between plant and animal cells, the structure and working of the plasma membrane and the many organelles that lie within, the controlling role of the nucleus, and finally how cells multiply through cell division - mitosis and meiosis.

4.1 THE CELL AS THE UNIT OF LIFE

The word 'cell' was coined by Robert Hooke in 1665 when he examined a thin slice of cork under his simple microscope and saw tiny box-like compartments that reminded him of the small rooms (cells) in a monastery. What Hooke actually saw were the empty walls of dead cork cells. A few years later Anton van Leeuwenhoek, using better lenses, was the first to see living cells and single-celled organisms, which he called 'animalcules'. The cell is described as the structural and functional unit of life: STRUCTURAL because all bodies are built of cells, and FUNCTIONAL because the basic life processes are carried out within the cell. Cells vary enormously in size and shape. The smallest cells are bacteria (Mycoplasma), only about 0.1 micrometre across, while the largest single cell is the ostrich egg. Whatever their size, cells share a common plan: a boundary membrane, a jelly-like cytoplasm, and genetic material (DNA).

4.2 THE CELL THEORY

The cell theory is one of the great unifying ideas of biology. In 1838 the German botanist Matthias Schleiden concluded that all plants are made of cells. In 1839 the German zoologist Theodor Schwann reached the same conclusion for animals and, together with Schleiden, proposed that the cell is the basic unit of structure of all living things. Their statement had one gap: it did not explain where new cells come from. This was supplied in 1855 by Rudolf Virchow, who declared 'Omnis cellula e cellula' - every cell arises from a pre-existing cell by division. The modern cell theory can be summarised in three statements: (1) all living organisms are composed of one or more cells; (2) the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life; and (3) all cells arise from pre-existing cells. A virus is an exception often discussed here - it has no cellular structure of its own and can multiply only inside a host cell, so it lies on the borderline of living and non-living.

4.3 PROKARYOTIC AND EUKARYOTIC CELLS

On the basis of the organisation of their nucleus and organelles, all cells fall into two great groups. PROKARYOTIC cells (pro = before, karyon = nucleus) are primitive cells that LACK a true, membrane-bound nucleus and lack membrane-bound organelles. Their single circular DNA molecule lies naked in the cytoplasm in a region called the NUCLEOID. Bacteria and cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) are prokaryotes. They are small (1-10 micrometre), have a rigid cell wall (made of peptidoglycan/murein in bacteria), possess only small 70S ribosomes, and carry out respiration on infoldings of the plasma membrane called mesosomes. Many bacteria also have a whip-like flagellum for movement and small extra rings of DNA called plasmids.

EUKARYOTIC cells (eu = true) are more advanced and possess a TRUE nucleus bounded by a nuclear envelope, together with a variety of membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus and (in plants) plastids. They are generally larger (10-100 micrometre) and have 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm. Protists, fungi, plants and animals are all eukaryotes. The evolution of the eukaryotic cell, with its compartments dividing labour among organelles, was a milestone that made complex multicellular life possible.

4.4 PLANT CELL AND ANIMAL CELL

Both plant and animal cells are eukaryotic and share the basic features of a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus and ribosomes. Yet they differ in several important ways. A PLANT CELL has a rigid CELL WALL of cellulose outside its plasma membrane, contains PLASTIDS (including green chloroplasts for photosynthesis), and usually has a single large central VACUOLE that pushes the cytoplasm to the edges and keeps the cell firm (turgid). A plant cell generally lacks centrioles. An ANIMAL CELL has NO cell wall (only the plasma membrane forms its boundary), has NO plastids, and its vacuoles, if present, are small and numerous. An animal cell contains a CENTROSOME with centrioles that help organise the spindle during cell division. These differences reflect their ways of life: plants make their own food and need support from rigid walls, whereas animals move about and need flexible boundaries.

4.5 THE PLASMA MEMBRANE

Every cell is enclosed by a thin, living PLASMA MEMBRANE (cell membrane, about 7.5-10 nanometre thick) that separates the inside of the cell from its surroundings and controls what enters and leaves. The widely accepted picture of its structure is the FLUID MOSAIC MODEL, proposed by Singer and Nicolson in 1972. According to this model the membrane is a double layer (bilayer) of PHOSPHOLIPID molecules in which PROTEIN molecules are embedded like a mosaic. Each phospholipid has a water-loving (hydrophilic) 'head' facing outward towards the watery medium and two water-hating (hydrophobic) 'tails' pointing inward, away from water. The lipid bilayer is FLUID - the molecules can move sideways - which is why the model is called 'fluid mosaic'. Some proteins (integral proteins) span the whole bilayer and act as channels or carriers; others (peripheral proteins) rest on the surface. Short carbohydrate chains attached to lipids and proteins on the outer face act as recognition markers. The membrane is described as SELECTIVELY PERMEABLE (semipermeable) because it allows only certain substances to pass.

TRANSPORT ACROSS THE MEMBRANE. Substances cross the plasma membrane by several routes. PASSIVE TRANSPORT needs no energy from the cell and moves substances DOWN a concentration gradient (from higher to lower concentration). (i) DIFFUSION is the net movement of molecules or ions from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration until they are evenly spread; gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide cross this way. (ii) OSMOSIS is the diffusion of WATER molecules across a selectively permeable membrane, from a region of higher water concentration (dilute solution) to a region of lower water concentration (concentrated solution). A cell placed in a hypotonic solution gains water and swells; in a hypertonic solution it loses water and shrinks (in plants the protoplasm pulls away from the wall - plasmolysis). (iii) FACILITATED DIFFUSION moves substances such as glucose down the gradient but with the help of specific carrier or channel proteins, still without energy. ACTIVE TRANSPORT moves substances AGAINST the concentration gradient (from lower to higher concentration) and therefore REQUIRES energy (ATP) and carrier proteins - for example the sodium-potassium pump. Large particles are moved in bulk by ENDOCYTOSIS (the membrane folds inward to engulf material - phagocytosis for solids, pinocytosis for liquids) and EXOCYTOSIS (a vesicle fuses with the membrane to expel material out of the cell).

4.6 THE CELL WALL

Outside the plasma membrane, plant cells, fungi, bacteria and algae possess a rigid CELL WALL. In plants it is made mainly of CELLULOSE (in fungi of chitin, in bacteria of peptidoglycan). The wall is non-living, freely permeable, and gives the cell shape, mechanical strength and protection, and prevents the cell from bursting when it takes in water. A young plant cell first lays down a thin, flexible PRIMARY WALL; as it matures a thicker SECONDARY WALL may be added inside. Neighbouring cells are cemented together by a middle lamella of calcium pectate, and fine cytoplasmic threads called PLASMODESMATA pass through the walls to connect adjacent cells.

4.7 THE CYTOPLASM AND ITS ORGANELLES

The CYTOPLASM is the jelly-like ground substance that fills the cell between the plasma membrane and the nucleus. Its fluid part is the cytosol, in which are suspended the various ORGANELLES ('little organs'), each a specialised structure with its own job. Together the organelles divide the work of the cell.

ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM (ER). The ER is a network of membrane-bound tubes and flattened sacs that runs through the cytoplasm and is continuous with the nuclear envelope. ROUGH ER is studded on its outer surface with ribosomes and is the site of PROTEIN synthesis and transport. SMOOTH ER lacks ribosomes and makes LIPIDS and steroids and helps detoxify harmful substances. The ER also forms a supporting internal framework and a transport highway.

GOLGI APPARATUS (Golgi complex). Discovered by Camillo Golgi, this organelle is a stack of flattened membranous sacs (cisternae). It receives proteins and lipids from the ER, then MODIFIES, PACKAGES and SORTS them into vesicles for secretion out of the cell or delivery to other organelles. It is often called the 'packaging and dispatching centre' of the cell, and it also forms lysosomes and helps build the cell wall/plate.

RIBOSOMES. Ribosomes are tiny granular structures made of RNA and protein, without a membrane. They are the sites of PROTEIN SYNTHESIS, joining amino acids in the order specified by messenger RNA. They occur free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough ER. Eukaryotic ribosomes are of the 80S type; those of prokaryotes and inside mitochondria and chloroplasts are the smaller 70S type.

LYSOSOMES. Lysosomes are small membrane-bound sacs, formed by the Golgi apparatus, that are filled with powerful DIGESTIVE (hydrolytic) enzymes. They digest food particles taken in by the cell and break down worn-out organelles. Because they can burst and digest the cell's own contents when the cell is damaged or dying, they are nicknamed the 'SUICIDAL BAGS' of the cell. They are common in animal cells.

PEROXISOMES. Peroxisomes are small membrane-bound organelles containing enzymes that carry out oxidation reactions; they break down fatty acids and destroy the toxic hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) produced in the cell using the enzyme catalase.

VACUOLES. A vacuole is a fluid-filled sac bounded by a single membrane (the tonoplast in plants). Plant cells usually have one LARGE central vacuole filled with cell sap that stores water, food, wastes and pigments and, by its turgor pressure, keeps the cell firm and gives support. Animal cells have small or no vacuoles.

CENTROSOME AND CENTRIOLES. The centrosome, found in animal cells near the nucleus, contains a pair of CENTRIOLES lying at right angles. During cell division the centrioles move to opposite poles and organise the SPINDLE FIBRES that separate the chromosomes. They also form the basal bodies of cilia and flagella. Higher plant cells usually lack centrioles.

4.8 MITOCHONDRIA - THE POWERHOUSE

Mitochondria (singular mitochondrion) are sausage-shaped organelles bounded by a DOUBLE membrane. The outer membrane is smooth, while the inner membrane is thrown into many folds called CRISTAE that greatly increase its surface area. The space enclosed by the inner membrane is filled with a fluid MATRIX. Mitochondria are the site of aerobic (cellular) RESPIRATION, in which food is oxidised and its energy is captured in molecules of ATP - the energy currency of the cell. For this reason mitochondria are called the 'POWERHOUSE of the cell'. They are semi-autonomous: they contain their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes and can make some of their own proteins and multiply by division - evidence that they may have arisen from ancient free-living bacteria (the endosymbiotic theory).

4.9 PLASTIDS

PLASTIDS are double-membrane organelles found only in PLANT cells and some protists. There are three main types. CHLOROPLASTS are green because they contain the pigment CHLOROPHYLL; they are the site of PHOTOSYNTHESIS, in which light energy is used to make food (glucose) from carbon dioxide and water. Inside a chloroplast the inner membrane encloses a fluid stroma in which are stacked coin-like thylakoids; a stack of thylakoids is called a GRANUM, and the chlorophyll sits on the thylakoid membranes. Like mitochondria, chloroplasts have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes. CHROMOPLASTS are coloured plastids (red, orange, yellow) that give colour to flowers and fruits and attract insects for pollination and animals for seed dispersal. LEUCOPLASTS are colourless plastids that STORE food - starch (in amyloplasts), oil or protein. One type of plastid can change into another (for example chloroplasts turn into chromoplasts as a tomato ripens).

4.10 THE NUCLEUS

The NUCLEUS, discovered by Robert Brown in 1831, is the largest organelle and the CONTROL CENTRE of the cell - it directs all the cell's activities and carries the hereditary information. It is usually spherical and bounded by a double-layered NUCLEAR ENVELOPE (nuclear membrane) perforated by many NUCLEAR PORES through which materials (such as RNA) pass between the nucleus and the cytoplasm; the outer membrane is continuous with the ER. Inside is a clear ground substance, the NUCLEOPLASM. Suspended in it is the CHROMATIN, a network of fine threads made of DNA and proteins (histones). When the cell prepares to divide, the chromatin condenses and coils into distinct rod-like CHROMOSOMES that carry the genes. A gene is a segment of DNA that controls a particular character. The nucleus also contains one or more dense rounded bodies called the NUCLEOLUS, which has no membrane and is the site where RIBOSOMES (ribosomal RNA) are made. Human body cells contain 46 chromosomes (23 pairs).

4.11 CELL DIVISION

Cells multiply by CELL DIVISION - one parent cell divides to form new (daughter) cells. Division allows organisms to grow, to replace old and damaged cells, and to reproduce. There are two main types: MITOSIS and MEIOSIS.

THE CELL CYCLE. A dividing cell passes through an orderly sequence of events called the cell cycle, which has two broad phases. The long INTERPHASE (the 'resting' phase) is the period between two divisions and is divided into three stages: the G1 phase (the cell grows and makes proteins and organelles), the S phase (the DNA is copied/replicated, so each chromosome now has two identical chromatids), and the G2 phase (the cell grows further and prepares for division). This is followed by the M PHASE, the actual division, made of MITOSIS (division of the nucleus) and CYTOKINESIS (division of the cytoplasm).

MITOSIS. Mitosis is the division of a body (somatic) cell that produces TWO daughter cells, each with the SAME number of chromosomes as the parent cell - it is an EQUATIONAL division. It occurs in four continuous stages. In PROPHASE the chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes (each with two sister chromatids joined at a centromere), the nuclear envelope and nucleolus begin to disappear, and the spindle starts to form. In METAPHASE the chromosomes line up single-file at the equator (middle) of the cell, attached to spindle fibres at their centromeres. In ANAPHASE the centromeres split and the two sister chromatids of each chromosome are pulled apart to OPPOSITE poles, becoming daughter chromosomes. In TELOPHASE the chromosomes reach the poles, uncoil back into chromatin, and a new nuclear envelope and nucleolus form around each group - two nuclei are now present. CYTOKINESIS then divides the cytoplasm (by a furrow in animal cells or a new cell plate in plant cells) to give two complete daughter cells. SIGNIFICANCE OF MITOSIS: it produces genetically identical cells, brings about growth and repair of tissues, replaces worn-out cells, and is the basis of asexual reproduction.

MEIOSIS. Meiosis is a special REDUCTION division that occurs only in the reproductive (germ) cells and forms the gametes (sperms and eggs). From one parent cell it produces FOUR daughter cells, each with HALF the chromosome number of the parent (the diploid 2n becomes haploid n). It involves TWO successive divisions, meiosis I and meiosis II, but the DNA is copied only once. In MEIOSIS I the homologous chromosomes (matching pairs) come together (synapsis) and exchange segments in a process called CROSSING OVER, which mixes the genes of the two parents and creates new combinations; then the homologous chromosomes separate, so the chromosome number is halved. MEIOSIS II resembles mitosis - the sister chromatids separate - giving four haploid cells in all. SIGNIFICANCE OF MEIOSIS: it keeps the chromosome number CONSTANT from generation to generation (because gametes are haploid, and fertilisation restores the diploid number), and crossing over together with the independent assortment of chromosomes produces VARIATION, which is the raw material for evolution.

SUMMARY

- The cell is the structural and functional unit of life; the term was coined by Robert Hooke (1665).
- Cell theory (Schleiden 1838, Schwann 1839, Virchow 1855): all organisms are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and every cell comes from a pre-existing cell.
- Prokaryotic cells lack a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (bacteria); eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus and organelles (protists, fungi, plants, animals).
- Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole; animal cells lack these but have a centrosome with centrioles.
- The plasma membrane is a selectively permeable fluid mosaic (Singer and Nicolson, 1972) of a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins; substances cross by diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion (passive), active transport (needs ATP), and endocytosis/exocytosis (bulk).
- Organelles and their jobs: rough ER (protein synthesis), smooth ER (lipids, detoxification), Golgi (modify/package/dispatch), ribosomes (protein synthesis), lysosomes ('suicidal bags', digestion), peroxisomes (break down H2O2), vacuoles (storage, turgor), centrosome (spindle).
- Mitochondria (double membrane, cristae) are the 'powerhouse', making ATP by respiration; plastids (chloroplast, chromoplast, leucoplast) occur only in plants.
- The nucleus (nuclear envelope with pores, chromatin, nucleolus) is the control centre; chromatin condenses into chromosomes that carry genes.
- The cell cycle is interphase (G1, S, G2) plus the M phase. Mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, cytokinesis) gives two identical diploid cells for growth and repair.
- Meiosis is a reduction division giving four haploid gametes; crossing over creates variation and the halved number keeps the species' chromosome number constant.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Cell: Structure and Function (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Answer short-answer questions briefly and long-answer questions in detail. Draw and label diagrams in words where asked.

questions.question: State the three main postulates of the cell theory and name the scientists associated with it.
questions.answer: The cell theory has three main postulates: (1) all living organisms are composed of one or more cells; (2) the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life; and (3) all cells arise from pre-existing cells by division. Matthias Schleiden (1838) established it for plants and Theodor Schwann (1839) for animals, and together they proposed the cell as the unit of structure. Rudolf Virchow (1855) added the third idea with his statement 'Omnis cellula e cellula' - every cell comes from a pre-existing cell.
questions.explanation: Three postulates plus the three contributors (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow).

questions.question: List any four differences between a prokaryotic and a eukaryotic cell.
questions.answer: (1) A prokaryotic cell has no true nucleus - its DNA lies free in the cytoplasm as a nucleoid - whereas a eukaryotic cell has a true nucleus bounded by a nuclear envelope. (2) Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles (no mitochondria, ER, Golgi), while eukaryotes possess them. (3) Prokaryotic cells are small (1-10 micrometre) and have 70S ribosomes; eukaryotic cells are larger (10-100 micrometre) with 80S ribosomes. (4) Prokaryotes are represented by bacteria and cyanobacteria; eukaryotes include protists, fungi, plants and animals.
questions.explanation: Any four contrasts: nucleus, organelles, size/ribosomes, examples.

questions.question: Describe the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane. Why is the membrane called selectively permeable?
questions.answer: The fluid mosaic model was proposed by Singer and Nicolson in 1972. According to it, the plasma membrane is made of a double layer (bilayer) of phospholipid molecules in which protein molecules are embedded like the pieces of a mosaic. Each phospholipid has a water-loving (hydrophilic) head facing the watery medium on either side and two water-hating (hydrophobic) tails pointing inward. The lipid bilayer is fluid - its molecules can move sideways - which gives the model its name. Integral proteins span the whole bilayer and act as channels or carriers, while peripheral proteins rest on the surface; short carbohydrate chains on the outer face act as recognition markers. The membrane is called selectively (or semi-) permeable because it does not allow all substances to pass: small and lipid-soluble molecules cross easily, while others are allowed in or out only through specific proteins, so the cell controls exactly what enters and leaves.
questions.explanation: Bilayer + embedded proteins + fluidity + selective permeability.

questions.question: Distinguish between diffusion and osmosis with one example of each.
questions.answer: Diffusion is the net movement of any molecules or ions from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration until they are evenly spread; it needs no membrane and no energy - for example, oxygen entering a cell or the smell of perfume spreading through air. Osmosis is a special case: it is the diffusion of only water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane, from a dilute solution (higher water concentration) to a concentrated solution (lower water concentration) - for example, water entering root-hair cells from the soil. Thus all osmosis is a kind of diffusion of water through a membrane, but not all diffusion is osmosis.
questions.explanation: Diffusion = any particle, no membrane needed; osmosis = only water across a semipermeable membrane.

questions.question: Why are lysosomes called the 'suicidal bags' of the cell? State one other function.
questions.answer: Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs filled with powerful digestive (hydrolytic) enzymes, formed by the Golgi apparatus. They are called 'suicidal bags' because, when a cell is damaged, worn out or dying, the lysosomes may burst and their enzymes digest the cell's own contents, killing the cell. Another important function is that they digest food particles taken into the cell by endocytosis and break down old, worn-out organelles, recycling their materials.
questions.explanation: Self-digestion on rupture = 'suicidal'; also digest food particles / worn-out organelles.

questions.question: Draw a labelled comparison in words: why is the mitochondrion called the powerhouse of the cell?
questions.answer: A mitochondrion is a double-membraned organelle: its outer membrane is smooth and its inner membrane is folded into finger-like cristae that project into a fluid matrix, greatly increasing the surface area. It is called the powerhouse of the cell because it is the site of aerobic (cellular) respiration, in which food such as glucose is oxidised and the energy released is stored in molecules of ATP - the energy currency the cell uses for all its activities. The large surface of the cristae carries the enzymes and carriers that make this ATP, so the mitochondrion generates most of the cell's usable energy.
questions.explanation: Double membrane + cristae + ATP production by respiration = powerhouse.

questions.question: Name the three types of plastids and state the function of each.
questions.answer: The three types of plastids are: (1) Chloroplasts - green plastids containing the pigment chlorophyll; they carry out photosynthesis, making food from carbon dioxide and water using light energy. (2) Chromoplasts - coloured (red, orange, yellow) plastids that give colour to flowers and fruits and so attract insects for pollination and animals for seed dispersal. (3) Leucoplasts - colourless plastids that store food such as starch (amyloplasts), oil or protein. Plastids occur only in plant cells.
questions.explanation: Chloroplast (photosynthesis), chromoplast (colour), leucoplast (storage).

questions.question: Explain the relationship between chromatin, chromosomes, DNA and genes.
questions.answer: Inside the nucleus is a network of fine threads called chromatin, made of DNA wound around proteins (histones). When the cell prepares to divide, this chromatin condenses and coils tightly to form distinct rod-like chromosomes. Each chromosome is therefore made of a long DNA molecule with its proteins. A gene is a small segment of that DNA that carries the code for a particular character (trait). So the order is: DNA is packaged with proteins as chromatin, chromatin condenses into chromosomes, and genes are specific segments of the DNA along the chromosome that control heredity.
questions.explanation: DNA + protein = chromatin -> condenses to chromosomes; genes = segments of DNA.

questions.question: Describe the four stages of mitosis and state its significance.
questions.answer: Mitosis is the division of a body cell into two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent. It has four continuous stages. PROPHASE: the chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids joined at a centromere; the nuclear envelope and nucleolus start to disappear and the spindle begins to form. METAPHASE: the chromosomes line up single-file at the equator (centre) of the cell, attached to spindle fibres at their centromeres. ANAPHASE: the centromeres split and the two sister chromatids of each chromosome are pulled to opposite poles, becoming daughter chromosomes. TELOPHASE: the chromosomes reach the poles, uncoil back into chromatin, and a new nuclear envelope and nucleolus form around each set, giving two nuclei; cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm. SIGNIFICANCE: mitosis produces genetically identical cells, brings about growth and the repair/replacement of worn-out cells, and is the basis of asexual reproduction.
questions.explanation: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase (+cytokinesis) with significance.

questions.question: What is crossing over and why is meiosis important for a species?
questions.answer: Crossing over is the exchange of corresponding segments between the non-sister chromatids of homologous (paired) chromosomes during meiosis I, when the homologues lie side by side (synapsis). It mixes the genes of the two parents and creates new gene combinations. Meiosis is important because it is a reduction division that produces haploid gametes (with half the chromosome number); when two gametes fuse at fertilisation the normal diploid number is restored, so the chromosome number of the species stays constant from generation to generation. In addition, crossing over and the independent assortment of chromosomes produce variation among offspring, which is the raw material for evolution.
questions.explanation: Crossing over = exchange of segments; meiosis keeps chromosome number constant and creates variation.

questions.question: Why is the cell called the structural and functional unit of life?
questions.answer: The cell is called the structural unit of life because the bodies of all living organisms, whether unicellular or multicellular, are built up of cells - they are the 'building blocks' of the body. It is called the functional unit because all the basic processes of life, such as taking in nutrients, releasing energy through respiration, growth, response to stimuli and reproduction, are carried out within cells. Thus both the structure and the working of every organism depend on cells.
questions.explanation: Structural = building blocks of the body; functional = life processes occur within.

questions.question: What is a virus, and why is it considered a borderline case of the cell theory?
questions.answer: A virus is an extremely small particle made of a nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat. It has no cellular structure of its own - no plasma membrane, cytoplasm or organelles - and it cannot carry out life processes independently. It can multiply only after entering a living host cell, where it uses the host's machinery. Because it shows the character of a living thing (reproduction) only inside a host but behaves like a non-living chemical outside, it lies on the borderline of living and non-living and is an exception to the cell theory.
questions.explanation: No cell structure of its own; multiplies only in a host, so borderline living/non-living.

questions.question: Give three differences between a plant cell and an animal cell.
questions.answer: (1) A plant cell has a rigid cellulose cell wall outside the plasma membrane, whereas an animal cell has only the plasma membrane as its boundary. (2) A plant cell contains plastids (including chloroplasts for photosynthesis); an animal cell has no plastids. (3) A mature plant cell usually has one large central vacuole, while an animal cell has small or no vacuoles. (In addition, animal cells have a centrosome with centrioles, usually absent in higher plant cells.)
questions.explanation: Cell wall, plastids, vacuole (and centriole) differences.

questions.question: Compare the size and ribosomes of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
questions.answer: Prokaryotic cells are small, usually 1-10 micrometre across, and contain only the smaller 70S ribosomes. Eukaryotic cells are generally larger, about 10-100 micrometre, and contain the larger 80S ribosomes in their cytoplasm (though their mitochondria and chloroplasts contain 70S ribosomes). So eukaryotic cells are bigger and have 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes, while prokaryotic cells are smaller with 70S ribosomes.
questions.explanation: Prokaryote: small, 70S; eukaryote: larger, 80S (organelles 70S).

questions.question: Distinguish between passive transport and active transport.
questions.answer: Passive transport is the movement of substances across the membrane DOWN a concentration gradient (from higher to lower concentration) and needs NO energy from the cell - it includes diffusion, osmosis and facilitated diffusion. Active transport is the movement of substances AGAINST the concentration gradient (from lower to higher concentration) and therefore REQUIRES energy in the form of ATP together with carrier proteins, for example the sodium-potassium pump. Thus the key differences are the direction relative to the gradient and the need for energy.
questions.explanation: Passive: down gradient, no ATP; active: against gradient, needs ATP.

questions.question: What is facilitated diffusion? How does it differ from simple diffusion?
questions.answer: Facilitated diffusion is the passive movement of substances (such as glucose or ions) across the plasma membrane DOWN their concentration gradient with the help of specific carrier or channel proteins, without using any energy. It differs from simple diffusion in that simple diffusion needs no proteins - molecules pass directly through the lipid bilayer - whereas facilitated diffusion requires a specific transport protein to carry the substance across, allowing water-soluble molecules that cannot cross the lipid layer easily to enter or leave the cell.
questions.explanation: Both passive/down gradient; facilitated needs carrier proteins, simple does not.

questions.question: Explain what happens when a red blood cell is placed in (a) a hypotonic and (b) a hypertonic solution.
questions.answer: (a) In a hypotonic solution (more dilute than the cell), water enters the cell by osmosis because the outside has a higher water concentration; the red blood cell swells and may eventually burst (haemolysis). (b) In a hypertonic solution (more concentrated than the cell), water leaves the cell by osmosis because the outside has a lower water concentration; the cell loses water and shrinks (crenation). This shows how osmosis moves water across the selectively permeable membrane depending on the surrounding concentration.
questions.explanation: Hypotonic: water in, swells/bursts; hypertonic: water out, shrinks.

questions.question: State four functions of the cell wall.
questions.answer: The cell wall (1) gives the cell a definite shape; (2) provides mechanical strength and rigidity so the plant can stand upright and its tissues are supported; (3) protects the delicate plasma membrane and the contents from injury and from attack by pathogens; and (4) prevents the cell from bursting when it takes in water by osmosis, since the rigid wall resists the swelling. Being freely permeable, it also lets water and dissolved substances pass to the membrane.
questions.explanation: Shape, strength/support, protection, prevents bursting.

questions.question: Describe the structure and functions of the endoplasmic reticulum.
questions.answer: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a network of membrane-bound tubes and flattened sacs running through the cytoplasm and continuous with the nuclear envelope. There are two kinds. Rough ER carries ribosomes on its outer surface and is the site of protein synthesis and transport. Smooth ER has no ribosomes and synthesises lipids and steroids and helps detoxify harmful substances. Together the ER also provides an internal supporting framework for the cell and acts as a transport system, carrying materials from one part of the cell to another.
questions.explanation: Network continuous with nuclear envelope; rough = protein, smooth = lipid/detox; also support/transport.

questions.question: Write the functions of the Golgi apparatus.
questions.answer: The Golgi apparatus is a stack of flattened membranous sacs (cisternae). Its functions are to receive proteins and lipids made by the endoplasmic reticulum, then to modify, package and sort them, and finally to dispatch them in vesicles - either for secretion out of the cell or for delivery to other organelles. It is therefore called the packaging and dispatching centre of the cell. It also forms lysosomes and, in plant cells, helps build the cell wall or cell plate during division.
questions.explanation: Modify, package, sort, dispatch; forms lysosomes; helps build cell wall.

questions.question: What are peroxisomes and what do they do?
questions.answer: Peroxisomes are small, single-membrane-bound organelles found in the cytoplasm that contain oxidative enzymes. They carry out oxidation reactions: they break down fatty acids and, importantly, they destroy the toxic hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) produced during metabolism, using the enzyme catalase, converting it to harmless water and oxygen. In plant seeds a related type, the glyoxysome, helps convert stored fat into sugar during germination.
questions.explanation: Oxidative organelles; catalase breaks down toxic H2O2; break down fatty acids.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a centrosome and its role in cell division.
questions.answer: The centrosome is a region found in animal cells, usually near the nucleus, that contains a pair of centrioles lying at right angles to each other. During cell division the centrioles move to opposite poles of the cell and organise the spindle fibres, the protein threads that attach to the chromosomes and pull them apart to the poles. Centrioles also form the basal bodies of cilia and flagella. Higher plant cells usually lack centrioles.
questions.explanation: Pair of centrioles at right angles; organise spindle during division.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a mitochondrion.
questions.answer: A mitochondrion is a small, sausage-shaped organelle bounded by a double membrane. The outer membrane is smooth and continuous, while the inner membrane is thrown into many finger-like folds called cristae that project inward and greatly increase the surface area. The space enclosed by the inner membrane is filled with a fluid matrix. The mitochondrion also contains its own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, so it is semi-autonomous.
questions.explanation: Double membrane, inner folded into cristae, fluid matrix, own DNA/70S ribosomes.

questions.question: Explain the internal structure of a chloroplast.
questions.answer: A chloroplast is a double-membraned plastid found in green plant cells. Inside the inner membrane is a fluid ground substance called the stroma. Suspended in the stroma are flattened, coin-shaped sacs called thylakoids; a stack of thylakoids is called a granum (plural grana), and several grana are connected by membranes. The green pigment chlorophyll lies on the thylakoid membranes, where it traps light energy for photosynthesis. The chloroplast also contains its own DNA and 70S ribosomes.
questions.explanation: Double membrane, stroma, thylakoids stacked into grana, chlorophyll on thylakoids.

questions.question: Why are mitochondria and chloroplasts described as semi-autonomous organelles?
questions.answer: Mitochondria and chloroplasts are called semi-autonomous because, unlike other organelles, each contains its own circular DNA and its own 70S ribosomes. This means they can make some of their own proteins and can grow and multiply by dividing, somewhat independently of the nucleus. However, they still depend on the nucleus for many of their proteins, so they are only partly (semi) self-governing. This independence supports the endosymbiotic theory that they arose from ancient free-living bacteria.
questions.explanation: Own DNA + 70S ribosomes, can make some proteins and divide, but still depend on nucleus.

questions.question: Distinguish between chromoplasts and leucoplasts.
questions.answer: Chromoplasts are coloured plastids containing pigments other than green - red, orange or yellow - which give colour to flowers and fruits and thus attract insects for pollination and animals for seed dispersal. Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that have no pigment and function in the storage of food - starch (in amyloplasts), oils or proteins - often in roots, tubers and seeds. So chromoplasts provide colour, while leucoplasts store food.
questions.explanation: Chromoplast = coloured, attracts; leucoplast = colourless, stores food.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the nucleus.
questions.answer: The nucleus is usually a spherical body and the largest organelle. It is bounded by a double-layered nuclear envelope (nuclear membrane) that is perforated by many nuclear pores, through which materials such as RNA pass between the nucleus and the cytoplasm; the outer membrane is continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum. Inside is a clear ground substance, the nucleoplasm, in which lies the chromatin - a network of fine threads of DNA and proteins that condenses into chromosomes at division. The nucleus also contains one or more dense bodies called nucleoli, where ribosomes are made.
questions.explanation: Nuclear envelope with pores, nucleoplasm, chromatin, nucleolus.

questions.question: What is the function of the nucleus in a cell?
questions.answer: The nucleus is the control centre of the cell. It directs and controls all the activities of the cell, such as growth, metabolism and division, by controlling the making of proteins. It also stores the hereditary information in its DNA (organised as chromosomes and genes) and passes this information to daughter cells during cell division, so it is responsible for inheritance of characters from one generation to the next.
questions.explanation: Controls cell activities and carries/transmits hereditary information.

questions.question: List the stages of interphase and state what happens in each.
questions.answer: Interphase, the long period between two divisions, has three stages. In the G1 phase the newly formed cell grows in size and makes proteins, enzymes and organelles. In the S (synthesis) phase the DNA is copied (replicated), so each chromosome comes to have two identical sister chromatids. In the G2 phase the cell grows further, makes more proteins and prepares the structures needed for division. After G2 the cell enters the M phase (mitosis and cytokinesis).
questions.explanation: G1 = growth; S = DNA replication; G2 = growth/preparation for division.

questions.question: State four points of significance of mitosis.
questions.answer: (1) Mitosis produces daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent cell, so it keeps the chromosome number and genetic make-up constant. (2) It brings about the growth of a multicellular organism by increasing the number of cells. (3) It repairs damaged tissues and replaces worn-out or dead cells (for example skin and blood cells). (4) It is the basis of asexual reproduction in many organisms (such as budding in yeast or regeneration).
questions.explanation: Identical cells, growth, repair/replacement, asexual reproduction.

questions.question: Give three differences between mitosis and meiosis.
questions.answer: (1) Mitosis occurs in body (somatic) cells, whereas meiosis occurs only in reproductive (germ) cells. (2) Mitosis produces two daughter cells, each with the same (diploid) chromosome number as the parent; meiosis produces four cells, each with half (haploid) the chromosome number. (3) Mitosis involves a single division and no crossing over, so daughter cells are genetically identical; meiosis involves two divisions and crossing over, producing genetic variation. (Thus mitosis is for growth and repair, meiosis is for gamete formation.)
questions.explanation: Cell type, number/ploidy of daughters, divisions and crossing over/variation.

questions.question: How does meiosis keep the chromosome number of a species constant?
questions.answer: In sexually reproducing organisms, meiosis halves the chromosome number when it forms the gametes: a diploid (2n) germ cell produces haploid (n) gametes. During fertilisation a male gamete (n) fuses with a female gamete (n) to form a zygote, restoring the full diploid number (2n). If gametes were diploid, the number would double every generation. Because meiosis reduces the number in gametes and fertilisation restores it, the chromosome number of the species stays the same from one generation to the next.
questions.explanation: Meiosis makes haploid gametes; fertilisation restores diploid number, keeping it constant.

questions.question: Trace the historical development of the cell theory, naming the key scientists and their contributions.
questions.answer: The cell theory developed gradually over about two centuries. In 1665 Robert Hooke examined a thin slice of cork under his microscope and saw tiny box-like compartments, which he named 'cells' after the small rooms of a monastery - though these were only the dead walls of cork. Soon after, Anton van Leeuwenhoek, using better lenses, became the first to observe living cells and single-celled organisms, which he called 'animalcules'. The theory itself took shape in the nineteenth century: in 1838 the botanist Matthias Schleiden concluded that all plants are made of cells, and in 1839 the zoologist Theodor Schwann reached the same conclusion for animals; together they proposed that the cell is the basic structural unit of all living things. Their theory could not, however, explain the origin of new cells. This gap was filled in 1855 by Rudolf Virchow, who declared 'Omnis cellula e cellula' - every cell arises from a pre-existing cell by division. Combining these ideas gives the modern cell theory: all organisms are made of one or more cells, the cell is the basic unit of structure and function, and all cells come from pre-existing cells.
questions.explanation: Hooke -> Leeuwenhoek -> Schleiden -> Schwann -> Virchow, with each contribution.

questions.question: Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells under the headings nucleus, organelles, size, ribosomes, cell wall and examples.
questions.answer: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells differ in several key features. NUCLEUS: a prokaryotic cell has no true nucleus - its single circular DNA lies naked in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid; a eukaryotic cell has a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear envelope. ORGANELLES: prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles (no mitochondria, ER or Golgi), and respire on membrane infoldings called mesosomes; eukaryotes possess many membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, ER, Golgi apparatus and (in plants) plastids. SIZE: prokaryotic cells are small, about 1-10 micrometre; eukaryotic cells are larger, about 10-100 micrometre. RIBOSOMES: prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes; eukaryotes have 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm (70S in their mitochondria and chloroplasts). CELL WALL: prokaryotic walls are made of peptidoglycan (murein); eukaryotic plant walls are of cellulose, fungal walls of chitin, and animal cells have no wall. EXAMPLES: bacteria and cyanobacteria are prokaryotes, while protists, fungi, plants and animals are eukaryotes.
questions.explanation: Systematic comparison across the six headings.

questions.question: Describe the different ways in which substances are transported across the plasma membrane.
questions.answer: Substances cross the plasma membrane by passive and active methods, and by bulk transport. PASSIVE TRANSPORT needs no energy and moves substances down a concentration gradient. (i) In simple diffusion molecules or ions move from a region of higher to lower concentration until evenly spread; gases like oxygen and carbon dioxide cross this way directly through the lipid bilayer. (ii) In osmosis only water moves across the selectively permeable membrane, from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one. (iii) In facilitated diffusion substances such as glucose move down the gradient but with the help of specific carrier or channel proteins, still without energy. ACTIVE TRANSPORT moves substances AGAINST the concentration gradient, from lower to higher concentration; it needs energy (ATP) and carrier proteins - a well-known example is the sodium-potassium pump. Finally, large particles are moved in bulk: in ENDOCYTOSIS the membrane folds inward to engulf material (phagocytosis for solids, pinocytosis for liquids), and in EXOCYTOSIS a vesicle fuses with the membrane to expel material out of the cell. Together these mechanisms let the cell control precisely what enters and leaves.
questions.explanation: Diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion (passive); active transport; endo/exocytosis.

questions.question: Describe the structure and functions of any four cytoplasmic organelles found in a cell.
questions.answer: Four important cytoplasmic organelles are the endoplasmic reticulum, the Golgi apparatus, ribosomes and lysosomes. The ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM is a network of membrane tubes and sacs continuous with the nuclear envelope; rough ER (with ribosomes) makes and transports proteins, and smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies harmful substances, as well as providing internal support and a transport route. The GOLGI APPARATUS is a stack of flattened sacs (cisternae) that receives materials from the ER, then modifies, packages and dispatches them in vesicles for secretion or delivery elsewhere; it also forms lysosomes - it is the cell's packaging and dispatching centre. RIBOSOMES are tiny granular structures of RNA and protein, with no membrane, that are the sites of protein synthesis, joining amino acids in the order set by messenger RNA; they occur free in the cytoplasm or on the rough ER. LYSOSOMES are membrane sacs of digestive enzymes, formed by the Golgi, that digest food particles and worn-out organelles and, on bursting in a damaged cell, digest the cell itself - hence 'suicidal bags'.
questions.explanation: ER, Golgi, ribosomes, lysosomes - structure and function of each.

questions.question: Explain why the mitochondrion is called the powerhouse of the cell, describing its structure and role.
questions.answer: The mitochondrion is called the powerhouse of the cell because it produces most of the cell's usable energy. STRUCTURE: it is a sausage-shaped organelle bounded by a double membrane. The outer membrane is smooth, while the inner membrane is folded into many finger-like cristae that project into a fluid matrix and greatly increase the inner surface area. The mitochondrion also has its own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes. ROLE: it is the site of aerobic (cellular) respiration. Here, food substances such as glucose are broken down step by step in the presence of oxygen, and the energy released is captured and stored in molecules of ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the energy currency of the cell. The large surface of the cristae carries the enzymes and electron carriers that make ATP, so a cell that needs much energy (such as a muscle cell) has many mitochondria. Because it generates this ATP that powers all the cell's activities, the mitochondrion is aptly named the powerhouse of the cell.
questions.explanation: Double membrane + cristae + matrix; respiration makes ATP = powerhouse.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the nucleus and explain how chromatin, chromosomes, genes and DNA are related.
questions.answer: The nucleus, discovered by Robert Brown, is the largest organelle and the control centre of the cell. STRUCTURE: it is bounded by a double-layered nuclear envelope perforated by many nuclear pores that allow materials such as RNA to pass between the nucleus and cytoplasm; the outer membrane is continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum. Inside is a clear ground substance, the nucleoplasm, containing the chromatin and one or more nucleoli. The nucleolus (which has no membrane) is the site where ribosomes are made. RELATIONSHIP: the chromatin is a network of fine threads made of DNA wound around proteins (histones). When the cell prepares to divide, this chromatin condenses and coils tightly to form distinct rod-like chromosomes. Each chromosome is therefore essentially a long, coiled DNA molecule with its proteins. Along the DNA lie the genes - each gene is a segment of DNA that carries the code for a particular character. So DNA + proteins form chromatin, chromatin condenses into chromosomes, and genes are functional segments of the DNA; through them the nucleus controls heredity.
questions.explanation: Nucleus structure + DNA->chromatin->chromosomes; genes = DNA segments.

questions.question: Describe the process of mitosis stage by stage and explain its significance.
questions.answer: Mitosis is the division of a body cell that produces two daughter cells, each with the same chromosome number as the parent (an equational division). It follows interphase, during which the DNA has already been copied so each chromosome has two sister chromatids. It occurs in four continuous stages. PROPHASE: the chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, each of two chromatids joined at a centromere; the nuclear envelope and nucleolus begin to disappear and the spindle fibres start to form. METAPHASE: the chromosomes move to and line up single-file at the equator of the cell, attached to spindle fibres at their centromeres. ANAPHASE: the centromeres split and the two sister chromatids of each chromosome are pulled apart to opposite poles, where they are now called daughter chromosomes. TELOPHASE: the chromosomes reach the poles and uncoil back into chromatin, the spindle breaks down, and a new nuclear envelope and nucleolus form around each group, giving two nuclei. CYTOKINESIS then divides the cytoplasm - by a cleavage furrow in animal cells or a cell plate in plant cells - into two complete daughter cells. SIGNIFICANCE: mitosis produces genetically identical cells, so it maintains the chromosome number; it brings about growth, repairs damaged tissues and replaces worn-out cells, and it forms the basis of asexual reproduction.
questions.explanation: Four stages + cytokinesis + significance (growth, repair, asexual reproduction).

questions.question: What is meiosis? Describe its two divisions in outline and explain its significance.
questions.answer: Meiosis is a special reduction division that takes place only in the reproductive (germ) cells and forms the gametes. From one diploid (2n) parent cell it produces four haploid (n) daughter cells, each with half the chromosome number. Although there are two successive divisions, the DNA is copied only once, before meiosis I. MEIOSIS I is the reduction division. The homologous chromosomes (matching pairs, one from each parent) come together in pairs (synapsis) and exchange corresponding segments in a process called crossing over, which mixes the parental genes. The homologous chromosomes then separate and move to opposite poles, so each new cell receives only one chromosome of each pair - the number is thereby halved. MEIOSIS II resembles an ordinary mitosis: in each of the two cells the sister chromatids separate, giving four haploid cells in all. SIGNIFICANCE: (1) by producing haploid gametes it keeps the chromosome number of the species constant, because fertilisation of two gametes restores the diploid number; and (2) crossing over together with the independent assortment of the chromosomes shuffles the genes and produces variation among the offspring, which is the raw material for evolution and the diversity of life.
questions.explanation: Reduction division; meiosis I halves number with crossing over, meiosis II separates chromatids; significance = constant number + variation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Robert Hooke, in 1665, cut a very thin slice of cork and examined it under his microscope. He saw many tiny, empty, box-like compartments packed together, which reminded him of the small rooms in a monastery, so he named them 'cells'. Later, better microscopes allowed Anton van Leeuwenhoek to see tiny living things moving in pond water. Over the next two centuries scientists like Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow built these observations into the cell theory.
(a) What did Hooke actually see in the cork?
(b) Why did he choose the name 'cell'?
(c) Whose work first revealed living cells?
(d) State any one postulate of the cell theory.
questions.answer: (a) Hooke saw only the empty walls of dead cork cells - box-like compartments, not living contents. (b) He named them 'cells' because the compartments looked like the small rooms (cells) in a monastery. (c) Anton van Leeuwenhoek was the first to see living cells and single-celled organisms ('animalcules') in pond water. (d) Any one: all organisms are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; every cell arises from a pre-existing cell.
questions.explanation: Tests understanding of the discovery of cells and the cell theory.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A student examines two cells under the microscope. Cell A is small (about 3 micrometre), has no membrane-bound nucleus - its DNA lies free in the cytoplasm - and has no mitochondria. Cell B is larger (about 40 micrometre), has a distinct nucleus bounded by a membrane, and contains mitochondria and a Golgi apparatus.
(a) Which cell is prokaryotic and which is eukaryotic?
(b) What is the region containing the DNA in cell A called?
(c) Name the type of ribosomes expected in cell A.
(d) Give one example each of an organism made of cell A type and of cell B type.
questions.answer: (a) Cell A is prokaryotic (no true nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles) and cell B is eukaryotic (true nucleus and organelles). (b) The DNA-containing region in cell A is the nucleoid. (c) Cell A has 70S ribosomes. (d) Cell A type: a bacterium (e.g. Escherichia coli) or a cyanobacterium; cell B type: any protist, fungus, plant or animal (e.g. an Amoeba or an onion cell).
questions.explanation: Applies prokaryote/eukaryote distinctions to described cells.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A peeled potato strip is placed in concentrated salt solution. After some time it becomes soft and flabby, and its cells are seen to have their protoplasm pulled away from the cell walls. When another strip is placed in pure water, it becomes firm and stiff.
(a) Name the process by which water moved in each case.
(b) What is the shrinking of the protoplasm away from the wall called?
(c) Why did the strip in salt solution become soft?
(d) Why did the strip in pure water become firm?
questions.answer: (a) The process is osmosis - the movement of water across the selectively permeable membrane. (b) The shrinking of the protoplasm away from the cell wall is called plasmolysis. (c) The salt solution is hypertonic, so water moved out of the cells by osmosis; the cells lost turgor and the strip became soft and flabby. (d) Pure water is hypotonic, so water moved into the cells by osmosis; the cells became turgid, making the strip firm and stiff.
questions.explanation: Applies osmosis, tonicity and plasmolysis to a practical situation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In a cell, a newly made protein is synthesised, then moves through a system of membranes where it is folded and modified. It is next packaged into a vesicle and finally released from the cell surface. Three organelles - ribosome, endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus - work in sequence to achieve this.
(a) On which organelle is the protein first made?
(b) Which ER (rough or smooth) transports the new protein?
(c) What does the Golgi apparatus do to the protein?
(d) Name the process by which the vesicle releases the protein out of the cell.
questions.answer: (a) The protein is first made on a ribosome (attached to the rough ER). (b) The rough endoplasmic reticulum transports the newly made protein. (c) The Golgi apparatus modifies, packages and sorts the protein and dispatches it in a vesicle. (d) The vesicle releases the protein out of the cell by exocytosis.
questions.explanation: Traces the secretory pathway through ribosome, ER and Golgi.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A muscle cell needs a great deal of energy to contract, and it is found to contain very many mitochondria. A green leaf cell, in contrast, contains numerous chloroplasts. Both organelles have a double membrane and their own DNA and 70S ribosomes.
(a) Why does a muscle cell contain many mitochondria?
(b) What process occurs in the chloroplasts of the leaf cell?
(c) What common feature suggests both organelles arose from ancient bacteria?
(d) Name the inner folds of the mitochondrion and the stacked sacs of the chloroplast.
questions.answer: (a) A muscle cell needs much energy (ATP) to contract, and mitochondria produce ATP by respiration, so many mitochondria supply the large energy demand. (b) Photosynthesis occurs in the chloroplasts - light energy is used to make food from carbon dioxide and water. (c) Both have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes (and a double membrane), which suggests they arose from free-living bacteria (endosymbiotic theory). (d) The inner folds of the mitochondrion are cristae; the stacked sacs of the chloroplast are grana (stacks of thylakoids).
questions.explanation: Links mitochondria/chloroplasts structure to function and origin.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The nucleus of a cell is bounded by a double membrane with many pores. Inside it a fine thread-like network is seen during the resting stage, but when the cell is about to divide, this network condenses into thick, short, rod-like bodies. A dense rounded structure is also present inside the nucleus.
(a) Name the double membrane and the pores.
(b) What is the thread-like network called?
(c) What are the rod-like bodies that form at division?
(d) Name the dense rounded structure and state its function.
questions.answer: (a) The double membrane is the nuclear envelope (nuclear membrane) and the openings are nuclear pores. (b) The thread-like network is the chromatin. (c) The rod-like bodies formed at division are the chromosomes. (d) The dense rounded structure is the nucleolus; it is the site where ribosomes (ribosomal RNA) are made.
questions.explanation: Identifies nuclear components and the chromatin-chromosome relationship.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A cell with 8 chromosomes divides by mitosis. Before division, during interphase, its DNA is copied. It then passes through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, and finally its cytoplasm divides.
(a) In which phase of interphase is the DNA copied?
(b) How many chromosomes will each daughter cell have?
(c) In which stage do the chromosomes line up at the equator?
(d) What is the division of the cytoplasm called?
questions.answer: (a) The DNA is copied in the S (synthesis) phase of interphase. (b) Each daughter cell will have 8 chromosomes - the same number as the parent, because mitosis is an equational division. (c) The chromosomes line up at the equator during metaphase. (d) The division of the cytoplasm is called cytokinesis.
questions.explanation: Applies the cell cycle and mitosis stages to a numerical example.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In the testis of an animal, certain cells with 24 chromosomes undergo meiosis to form sperms. The process involves two successive divisions, during the first of which paired chromosomes exchange parts before separating.
(a) How many chromosomes will each sperm contain?
(b) How many cells are formed from one such parent cell?
(c) Name the exchange of parts between paired chromosomes.
(d) State one significance of this exchange.
questions.answer: (a) Each sperm will contain 12 chromosomes - half of 24 - because meiosis is a reduction division. (b) Four cells (sperms) are formed from one parent cell. (c) The exchange of parts between paired (homologous) chromosomes is called crossing over. (d) Crossing over produces new combinations of genes, giving rise to variation among the offspring (raw material for evolution).
questions.explanation: Applies meiosis to gamete formation and variation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
White blood cells can move towards bacteria, surround them by folding their membrane inward, and engulf them into a vesicle. Inside the cell, small sacs full of digestive enzymes then fuse with the vesicle and break the bacteria down.
(a) Name the process by which the cell engulfs the bacteria.
(b) Name the sacs full of digestive enzymes.
(c) Which organelle forms these sacs?
(d) Why are these sacs sometimes called 'suicidal bags'?
questions.answer: (a) The engulfing of the solid bacteria by infolding of the membrane is phagocytosis (a type of endocytosis). (b) The sacs full of digestive enzymes are lysosomes. (c) Lysosomes are formed by the Golgi apparatus. (d) They are called 'suicidal bags' because, if the cell is damaged or dying, the lysosomes may burst and their enzymes digest the cell's own contents, killing it.
questions.explanation: Connects endocytosis and lysosome function in immune defence.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A plant cell and an animal cell are compared. The plant cell has a rigid outer covering, green bodies in its cytoplasm and a large fluid-filled sac in the centre. The animal cell lacks all three but has a structure near its nucleus that helps in division.
(a) Name the rigid outer covering of the plant cell.
(b) Name the green bodies and state their function.
(c) Name the large central sac and one of its functions.
(d) Name the structure in the animal cell that helps in division.
questions.answer: (a) The rigid outer covering of the plant cell is the cell wall (made of cellulose). (b) The green bodies are chloroplasts; they carry out photosynthesis (making food using light energy). (c) The large central sac is the (central) vacuole; it stores cell sap (water, food, wastes, pigments) and, by its turgor pressure, keeps the cell firm and gives support. (d) The structure in the animal cell that helps in division is the centrosome (with its centrioles), which organises the spindle.
questions.explanation: Contrasts plant and animal cell structures and their functions.
